title: The Vindolanda birthday invitation
hook: A Roman party invitation holds some of the oldest Latin handwriting by a woman.
peek: Around AD 100, near what became Hadrian's Wall, Claudia Severa invited her friend Sulpicia Lepidina to her birthday party. A scribe wrote most of the note on a thin wooden tablet, but Claudia added a few lines in her own hand.
lede: At the Roman fort of Vindolanda in northern England, archaeologists have found hundreds of thin wooden writing tablets, preserved in waterlogged, oxygen-free ground. One of the best loved, from around AD 100, is a birthday invitation. Claudia Severa asks her friend Sulpicia Lepidina to visit on 11 September, adding that the day will be more enjoyable if she comes.

bullets.text: Most of the invitation was written by a scribe, in neat lettering. At the end Claudia added a farewell in a different, less practised hand, calling Lepidina her sister. It is among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman.

Lepidina was the wife of Flavius Cerialis, commander of the garrison at Vindolanda. Other letters to her from Claudia survive too, showing a warm friendship between two officers' wives on the edge of the empire.
The tablets are slivers of wood about the size of a postcard, written in ink. Robin Birley's team began finding them in 1973, and many, including the invitation, are now in the British Museum.
